Iconoclast Controversy
eye-KON-oh-klast kon-truh-VUR-see
noun phrase (a Byzantine dispute over images)
From the Greek eikon (image) and klastes (breaker); the eighth- and ninth-century Byzantine dispute between the iconoclasts (image-breakers) and the iconodules (image-venerators) over the use of images in worship.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Iconoclast Controversy was the long and bitter dispute that shook the Byzantine church in the eighth and ninth centuries over the place of images in Christian worship. On one side stood the iconoclasts—the “image-breakers”—who, beginning under the emperors, condemned the making and venerating of images of Christ and the saints as a breach of the second commandment, and removed or destroyed them. On the other stood the iconodules, the “image-servers,” who defended the veneration of icons, arguing from the incarnation that the invisible God, having taken visible flesh, might now be depicted, and distinguishing the honour given to the image from the worship due to God alone. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) sided with the venerators, and the practice of icon veneration became fixed in the East. The dictionary takes its stand plainly with the iconoclasts on the substance of the matter, though not with every excess of mob and emperor. The second commandment forbids making any graven image or likeness to bow down before it, and the regulative principle of worship holds that God is to be served only as He has appointed in His Word. The bowing to, kissing of, and burning incense before images of Christ and the saints, however the venerators may distinguish veneration from worship, is the very thing Scripture condemns: God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth, not before the work of men's hands. The argument from the incarnation does not overturn the commandment, for no man hath seen God at any time, and the Son who declared the Father did so in the gospel, not in painted wood. The dictionary honours the iconoclasts' zeal for the holiness of worship and the second commandment, and counts the triumph of image veneration a sad and lasting corruption.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The eighth- and ninth-century Byzantine dispute over images in worship; the dictionary sides with the iconoclasts on the second commandment and the regulative principle, counting the triumph of icon veneration (Second Nicaea, 787) a lasting corruption.

ICONOCLAST CONTROVERSY, noun phrase. [Greek eikon, image, and klastes, breaker.] The Byzantine dispute over images.

The iconoclasts condemned and destroyed images of Christ and the saints.

The iconodules defended their veneration, appealing to the incarnation.

The Second Council of Nicaea (787) sided with the venerators.

The dictionary sides with the iconoclasts on the second commandment (Exodus 20:4-5).

📖 Key Scripture

Ex 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Ex 20:5 — "Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;"

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

De 4:15 — "Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The triumph of icon veneration at the Second Council of Nicaea (787) fixed in the East a breach of the second commandment; the dictionary stands with the iconoclasts and the regulative principle of worship.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the second commandment and the regulative principle of worship: that God is to be worshipped only as He has appointed in His Word, and that men shall not make any graven image or likeness to bow down before it. The corruption to be named is the veneration of icons that triumphed in the East. The iconodules defended bowing to, kissing, and censing images of Christ and the saints, arguing from the incarnation that the God who took visible flesh may now be depicted, and distinguishing the honour paid to the image from the worship due to God alone. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 enshrined this practice, and the dictionary judges it a sad and lasting corruption of pure worship.

The dictionary sides with the iconoclasts on the substance, though not with every violence of mob or emperor. The distinction between veneration and worship cannot rescue the practice, for the second commandment forbids the very act of bowing before the likeness, whatever name be given the inward intent. The appeal to the incarnation fails: no man hath seen God at any time, Israel saw no manner of similitude at Horeb lest they corrupt themselves, and the Son declared the Father in the gospel preached, not in painted wood and gilded panel. God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth. The dictionary honours the iconoclasts' zeal for the holiness of worship, counts the Reformers their heirs in stripping the images from the churches, and holds that the honour of God is guarded only where worship is offered as He commanded, neither more nor less.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From eikon (image) and klastes (breaker), “image-breaker”; the Byzantine party that opposed the iconodules (“image-servers”) in the controversy over images in worship.

expand to see more

Eikon, Greek, “image”; klastes, “breaker.”

Iconoclasts, the “image-breakers” who opposed images in worship.

Iconodules, the “image-servers” who defended their veneration.

The Second Council of Nicaea (787) fixed icon veneration in the East.

Rooted in the second commandment and the regulative principle of worship.

"He showed the distinction of veneration from worship cannot rescue the bowing Scripture forbids."

"She named the triumph of icon veneration at Nicaea (787) a lasting corruption of pure worship."
